Hesse
HESS
n. (the landgraviate whose prince called the Marburg Colloquy, founded the first Protestant university, and disgraced the cause by his bigamy)
German Hessen, from the Chatti, the Germanic people of the region named by Tacitus; Latin Hassia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hesse is the German principality whose landgrave did the Reformation its greatest political service and its greatest private injury. Philip of Hesse took the Reformation into his lands from 1526, held the Homberg Synod in that year and had a church order drafted by Francois Lambert, founded Marburg in 1527 as the first university established as a Protestant foundation, and was with the Elector of Saxony the chief organiser of the Schmalkaldic League, the defensive alliance that kept the evangelical states in being. He saw further than most that the Lutheran and the Swiss must not divide, and it was he who summoned Luther, Zwingli, Bucer, Oecolampadius and Melanchthon to the Marburg Colloquy of October 1529; they agreed on fourteen articles and parted over the fifteenth, the presence of Christ in the Supper. In 1540 Philip, already married, took a second wife, having extracted from Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer a secret and shameful counsel permitting it as a dispensation; the matter became public, cost him his political standing, and gave the Reformation's enemies their most useful scandal. The dictionary enters Hesse because the record must carry both halves: the colloquy and the league, and the bigamy and the theologians who signed it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a landgrave as a German count having jurisdiction over a territory; a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse; bigamy as the crime of having two wives at once; and a dispensation as an exemption from a law.

expand to see more

LANDGRAVE, n. In Germany, a count or earl; originally an officer with jurisdiction over a territory.

COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.

BIGAMY, n. The crime of having two wives at once; the having of a second wife while the first is living.

DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by law.

LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.

Key Scripture

Mat 19:5 — "And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?"

Mal 2:14 — "Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant."

Gal 2:11 — "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

Pro 28:13 — "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy."

Modern Corruption

Landgraviate whose prince founded Marburg in 1527, called the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 and organised the Schmalkaldic League, and whose bigamy in 1540 disgraced the cause.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is a pastoral counsel bent to suit a prince, and it is ours to own. Philip of Hesse pressed Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer for permission to take a second wife, and they gave it in a written and secret opinion, advising that the thing be concealed. The Lord's word on marriage admits no such dispensation: “they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5), and the prophet's rebuke to men who dealt treacherously with the wife of their youth stands over the whole transaction, for the Lord “hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth” (Mal 2:14).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a reformer who will not be rebuked has stopped reforming, and the apostolic precedent is public: Paul “withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) when Peter was to be blamed. No one did that for Philip until the secret was out and the damage done. The right course was open and was not taken, for “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13), and the dictionary records the counsel as a sin of the Reformers and not merely an embarrassment of the Reformation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; Hebrew bagad (H898), to deal treacherously; Greek anthistemi (G436), to withstand.

expand to see more

Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh, the body; “they twain shall be one flesh”, Matthew 19:5.

Greek proskollao (G4347) — to glue to, to cleave fast; “shall cleave to his wife”, Matthew 19:5.

Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness, one who testifies; “hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth”, Malachi 2:14.

Greek anthistemi (G436) — to set against, to withstand; “I withstood him to the face”, Galatians 2:11.

Hebrew azab (H5800) — to forsake, to leave off; “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy”, Proverbs 28:13.

Usage

"“they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5) — the secret counsel of 1540 permitting a second wife."

"“I withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) — the rebuke the landgrave's theologians did not give him."

"“whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13) — a scandal concealed until it could not be."
